bbe_format: Five independent True/False statements (A–E) per case; variable number of TRUE statements; C(n,r)/P(n,r) notation; narrative word-problem stems.

tasks.title: The Assessment Poster
tasks.context: For a campus assessment fair, ten letter tiles spelling the word ASSESSMENT (A, S, S, E, S, S, M, E, N, T) are placed in a bag and drawn out one at a time to form a poster headline in a row. Tiles for the same letter are indistinguishable from one another. The word contains four S's, two E's, and one each of A, M, N, and T. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of distinct posters that can be formed is 75,600.
The probability that all four S's end up adjacent to each other is 1/30.
The probability that the two E's end up adjacent to each other is greater than 1/4.
The probability that all four S's are adjacent AND the two E's are adjacent (simultaneously) is less than 1%.
The probability that M and T end up adjacent to each other equals the probability that the two E's end up adjacent to each other.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Treating the four S's as one block leaves 7 units with the E's still repeated, giving 7!/2! = 2,520, so P = 2,520/75,600 = 1/30. Formula: P(S's adjacent) = [7!/2!] / [10!/(4!·2!)] = 1/30
FALSE — P(E's adjacent) = 15,120/75,600 = 1/5 = 0.20, which is not greater than 1/4 = 0.25. Formula: P(E's adjacent) = 1/5, not > 0.25
TRUE — Both equal 15,120/75,600 = 1/5. Formula: P(M,T adjacent) = 2·[9!/(4!·2!)] / [10!/(4!·2!)] = 1/5 = P(E's adjacent)

tasks.title: The National Lottery
tasks.context: In a national lottery, six distinct winning numbers are drawn uniformly at random without replacement from the integers 1 through 49. A player has already filled in one ticket with six chosen numbers. 'Matching k numbers' means that exactly k of the player's six numbers appear among the six winning numbers. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of distinct possible draws is greater than 13 million.
The probability that the player matches exactly 3 numbers is greater than 2%.
The probability that the player matches exactly 0 numbers is greater than 40%.
The probability of matching all 6 numbers (the jackpot) is greater than 1 in 10 million.
The probability of matching exactly 3 numbers is more than 15 times the probability of matching exactly 4 numbers.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — C(49,6) = 13,983,816 > 13 million. Formula: Total draws = C(49, 6)
FALSE — P(exactly 3) ≈ 1.765%, not greater than 2%. Formula: C(6,3)·C(43,3)/C(49,6) ≈ 1.765%
FALSE — Jackpot ≈ 1 in 14.0 million, which is not greater than 1 in 10 million. Formula: 1/C(49,6) ≈ 7.15×10⁻⁸ < 10⁻⁷

tasks.title: The Student Project Team
tasks.context: A lecture group consists of 10 computer-science (CS) students and 8 business students (18 students total). The instructor selects 4 of the 18 students completely at random to form a project team. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of possible 4-person teams is 3,060.
The probability that the team contains exactly 2 CS and 2 business students is greater than 40%.
The probability that all 4 team members are business students is less than 3%.
The probability that at least one CS student is on the team is less than 95%.
The probability that CS students form a majority of the team (3 or 4 of the 4 seats) is greater than the probability that exactly 2 seats go to CS students.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — C(18,4) = 3,060. Formula: Total teams = C(18, 4)
FALSE — P(at least 1 CS) ≈ 97.71%, not less than 95%. Formula: 1 − C(8,4)/C(18,4)
FALSE — CS majority ≈ 38.24% < exactly-2 ≈ 41.18%. Formula: Compare C(10,3)·C(8,1)+C(10,4) vs C(10,2)·C(8,2)

tasks.title: Tennis Club Pairings
tasks.context: At a tennis club meeting, 12 players attend. Before the matches begin, every pair of players shakes hands exactly once as a warm-up greeting. Afterward, the 12 players are paired up completely at random into 6 simultaneous singles matches for round 1 (each player plays exactly one opponent). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of handshakes exchanged during the warm-up is 66.
The number of distinct ways to pair the 12 players into 6 round-1 matches is 10,395.
The probability that two specific players, Anna and Ben, are paired against each other in round 1 is 1/6.
The probability that one specific complete pairing (a predetermined list of exactly which 6 pairs play each other) is the one that occurs is 1/1,000.
If the club instead had 6 players, the number of ways to pair them into 3 round-1 matches would be 15.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — P(Anna plays Ben) = 1/11, not 1/6. Formula: 1/(12−1) = 1/11

tasks.title: The Gala Dinner
tasks.context: At a gala dinner, 4 men and 4 women (8 distinct people total) are seated uniformly at random in a single row of 8 chairs. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of possible seating arrangements is 40,320.
The probability that the genders strictly alternate along the row (man–woman–man–woman… or woman–man–woman–man…) is exactly 1/35.
The probability that all four women sit in four consecutive seats is greater than 10%.
The probability that two specific guests end up in adjacent seats is exactly 1/4.
The probability that both end seats are occupied by women is greater than 20%.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — 2·7!/8! = 1/4. Formula: P(two specific adjacent) = 2/n with n = 8

tasks.title: The Coat Check
tasks.context: Six guests check identical-looking coats at a restaurant. On the way out, the attendant returns the six coats completely at random — each of the 6! permutations of coats-to-guests is equally likely. A guest is said to receive their own coat when the permutation fixes that guest's position. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The total number of ways the coats can be returned is 720.
The probability that no guest receives their own coat is greater than 40%.
The probability that exactly two guests receive their own coats is greater than 15%.
The probability that exactly five guests receive their own coat is greater than 0.
The probability that at least one guest receives their own coat is less than 50%.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Exactly two fixed points: C(6,2)·!4 = 15·9 = 135, so P = 135/720 = 18.75% > 15%. Formula: P(exactly 2 fixed) = C(6,2)·!4 / 6! = 135/720 = 18.75%
FALSE — Exactly 5 fixed points is impossible (probability 0). Formula: P(exactly n−1 fixed points) = 0
FALSE — P(at least one own) = 1 − 265/720 ≈ 63.19%, not < 50%. Formula: 1 − !6/6!
